basins.name: Itajaí
basins.description: In Santa Catarina, the Itajaí River basin cuts across one of southern Brazil’s most dynamic economic regions, but is also a region prone to recurring flooding. In 2008, intense rainfall, landslides, and severe infrastructure damage reshaped how the region understands risk. The balance between economic development, environmental fragility, and repeated extreme events makes a case for why stronger risk management, climate adaptation, and territorial resilience are essential.

basins.name: Alto Tietê
basins.description: Home to São Paulo and 39 other municipalities, over 20 million people depend on the Alto Tietê basin, which underpins the country’s most significant center of employment, industrial production, and economic activity. Water demand is approximately double availability, so the region must rely on inter-basin transfers, notably from the Cantareira System, to meet its needs. Intense land use, combined with persistent challenges related to water quality, urban drainage, flooding, and climate change variability, acutely illustrates the need to integrate urban planning, water‑resource management, and climate adaptation.

basins.name: Paraíba do Sul
basins.description: The Paraíba do Sul River Basin spans three states and serves as the principal industrial hub of the Southeast region, accounting for an estimated 12% of national GDP. While supplying water to over 14 million inhabitants, it also critically sustains ecosystems and maintains biodiversity. Robust governance and integrated planning are helping build resilience to overcome the challenge of harmonizing economic growth, environmental conservation, and water security.

basins.name: São Francisco
basins.description: Among Brazil’s most strategic hydrological regions, the São Francisco River Basin encompasses roughly 8% of Brazil’s territory, extending across seven states and serves as the principal source of surface water for the Northeast. The São Francisco River Integration Project has served over 12 million people and reshaped the economy of the Northeastern interior, now Brazil’s largest center for irrigated fruit cultivation and exports. In addition, it is host to a major hydroelectric complex. However, recurrent droughts and reliance on extensive hydraulic infrastructure demonstrate the value of resilience strategies in water‑scarce and climate‑vulnerable territories.

basins.name: Piancó–Piranhas–Açu
basins.description: In the semi-arid hinterland of the sertão, the Piancó-Piranhas-Açu River Basin constitutes the economic and social foundation of this sparsely populated region spanning two states. It is also one of Brazil’s regions that is most vulnerable to climate change, experiencing recurring extreme droughts that make watercourses dry up completely. This pronounced water deficit has led to the construction of extensive infrastructure to support domestic and agricultural water supply, including reservoirs and inter-basin transfer canals that convey water from the São Francisco River.

basins.name: Tocantins–Araguaia
basins.description: Critically located between the Cerrado and the Amazon biomes, the Tocantins-Araguaia River Basin has emerged as one of the nation’s foremost economic, logistical, and energy frontiers. This waterway connects the Center-West of Brazil to northern ports, forming a strategic and lower-cost transportation route for grain and mineral exportation. As a leading frontier of agricultural and livestock expansion, the region faces intense pressure from deforestation and large-scale irrigation. It also contains one of Brazil’s major hydroelectric complexes. The rapid pace of land-use transformation calls for integrated planning capable of balancing economic growth, environmental protection, and long-term water security.
